item.title: Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health the Most
item.description:
Statistically, men are less often diagnosed with depression than women, and yet are more likely to commit suicide. There is something important about male mental health that lurks in the gap between these two facts: that men are seemingly less depressed than women, but take their own lives in far greater numbers every year.

This disparity raises the question: “Why is it that more men are dealing with depression but not talking about it? Why do more men not seek help when they experience depression?”

Many men suffer silently because they simply don’t have the vocabulary to describe their struggle, while others are just trying to get by without having to ask for help. Men have been raised to believe that asking for help is a sign of weakness, or sold lies about masculinity and mental health. However, the truth of God’s Word will ultimately set men free if they can learn to tune into the right “voices” and obtain correct information.

No man wants to feel impotent or victimized, but the truth is that men do struggle. Being a man does not mean being on par with gods and angels. They bleed, they get hurt, life affects them, and it is only when men acknowledge that they’re stuck or struggling that they can find the help they need to heal or move on.

Maybe it’s time to address the shame and fear that have been holding men back, assess the situation they’re in, and talk to each other about the struggle. In this way, men can begin to make progress as men and as individuals by talking privately and openly with a trusted friend, or even accessing the power of a group of men sharing similar experiences.

You are never truly alone unless you want to be. Jesus Himself was an example of not carrying a burden alone. He shared the challenges he faced with His disciples openly and lovingly, and they responded to Him in kind.

Individuals and the Collective

For the most part, men have been taught that vulnerability is a kind of weakness. To be masculine is to be “strong,” and to be “strong” equates to handling life’s difficulties on their own.

From the youngest age, men are taught that boys don’t cry and that any emotion other than anger and apathy is for the weak. Even the milder depictions of masculinity that were modeled were sometimes toxic, if only because they were built on incomplete understandings of male mental health.

Boys do cry, show hurt, sadness, tenderness, and affection, along with the whole range of human emotions. So do men. Men are mentally, emotionally, and physically complex by design, and that is an important and powerful part of God’s design. Besides this, men are all individuals with unique experiences, insights, skills, and traumas.

Only when people begin to understand and accept men as individuals can we begin to figure out where each of us fits into the collective. There might be some broad cultural ideals that men are expected to meet, but we will each reach these goals by taking our own unique paths to them.

The man who uses his hands to build houses in the village is no less valuable than the man who plants crops and flowers, and no less valuable than the disabled man who is only able to tell stories and speak sense to the next generation.

In the same way, men who show more masculine physical traits and/or limited emotional expression could learn from men around them that there are many benefits to softer, more sensitive emotions, which they often avoid. Each man has different roles, unique struggles, personal pressure points, and each of these things determines value as individuals first and as men second.

At the end of the day, each man is responsible for himself, his spouse or partner, and his family. Some men’s greatest achievement in life is that they are patient and kind toward others, and generous and loving toward themselves as well, even while maintaining ordinary jobs and receiving minimum wage.

Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health

Regardless of your unique skills, personality, or life experiences, as a man, you will face one or more of the following struggles, statistically speaking. Male mental health is affected by a collection of similar struggles that seem to reach across generations and cultures.

These are the things that we must face head-on, be vocal and honest about as we navigate them, and find our way of getting through them to avoid being part of the tragic statistics. Unfortunately, there is no road map or blueprint for how to get through this stuff. Each man must do his best, help his brothers, accept help from those who love him, and keep going.

Unemployment and Work Struggles

The one aspect of life where men draw our worth from the most is our contribution to society. Men know that if we don’t work, we don’t eat; that’s just how the world works. Sadly, life isn’t just as simple as finding a well-paying job and doing that until retirement.

Sometimes it takes decades to find something that they enjoy doing and are good at, and even then, the job market is so unstable that they aren’t guaranteed employment, a healthy work environment, or a manageable workload.

Few things negatively impact male mental health more than unemployment, especially when it lasts for months and years. Criticism and harsh words around this situation can often cut the deepest in a man’s security in a relationship and his self-image.

At the core, men not only need security and stability, but also to know that they are making a valuable contribution somewhere. They need to know that they are seen and appreciated, even as they struggle. It is not weak or shameful to need to feel valued; in fact, it is a sign that they see their own value.

Money Problems

Men work to contribute something valuable, but also to find financial stability. They might not be able to find a job that offers both, but if they can’t at least find a way to put food on the table and pay bills, their mental health will plummet in a sea of anxiety and fear. When there is the added pressure of having a family to provide for, the strain of not making enough money is enough to sink any man’s health.

Relationship Issues

God said right at the start that it wasn’t good for man to be alone. Many men have learned to cope well with being on their own, but for those with marriages and families, nothing is more tumultuous than a family torn apart by divorce or separation.

Male mental health is often at its lowest when there is a dramatic change in the family and a lack of social support through these changes. Regardless of the cause of these struggles, no man can navigate these experiences alone, and some don’t make it through these struggles alive.

Isolation

Men are more likely to try to cope privately and silently with their problems. Many grew up with fathers who were fixers, who never asked for help and who never modeled vulnerability and humility. Male mental health suffers most in stubborn silence and in isolation.

If you find yourself without a decent support system or without people to talk to or listen to your experiences, make changes as soon as possible. Having even a single confidant or trusted friend can make all the difference to male mental health.

Stigma

Perhaps you are trying to navigate life alone because that’s what was expected of you. That is the case for many men. Here’s the thing about stereotypes and toxic masculinity, though: it kills. If you have spent your entire life internalizing your struggles and externalizing your aggression, you have missed out on some of the most fundamental experiences of being a man.

Brotherhood, vulnerability, accountability, and humility are all vital aspects of masculinity, yet many are bound by misguided, cruel, and damaged depictions of manhood. Lies will keep you bound in fear, but the truth will release you to be the best version of yourself possible.

Discover Better Mental Health

If you have never asked for help or opened up about your struggles, this is your challenge to do so. The idea of opening up to someone might fill you with dread, and you might not even have the language to describe what you are going through. Counselors and therapists are impartial, patient, and non-judgmental third parties who provide a safe space in which you can be completely honest.

You can start by consulting our online catalog of counselors, where you will hopefully find someone suitable, or you may ask our reception team to help connect you with someone. You no longer have to struggle alone; there is someone out there who will listen without judgment.

item.title: Children’s Mental Health: Five Toxic Phrases NOT to Say to Your Kids
item.description:
Most parents strive to be loving, supportive, and caring to their children. They read self-help and parenting books to learn how to be the best parents they can be. They painstakingly curate friendships to help their kids thrive and run to the rescue whenever someone says something offensive to them. They may even rehearse pep talks and thoughtfully craft sentimental birthday card messages.

And yet, even the most well-intentioned parents fall short of their own parenting ideals sometimes. In stressful moments, you might not take the time to consider your words. You might repeat phrases you heard growing up that seem to work in specific situations. Other times you might not be mindful of your words at all.

Some clichés and rote statements seem to be inherited as they have been used and reused by parents for generations. And they can creep out of your mouth without much forethought.

They might sound harmless, even motivating, but these common, seemingly benign comments can negatively impact children’s mental health and shape how your children view themselves and their place in the family.

Why can’t you be more like ____?

How does the old saying go: “Comparison is the thief of joy.”

If you’re a parent and you don’t think your child is quite living up to their potential or is making questionable choices, you might be tempted to use peer pressure to motivate them into better choices. You point out the good things you see in others their age as a means of motivation.

To you, you’re showing them a good example of proper behavior. To them, you’re favoring someone else over them. While you might think that you’re motivating your child, you are likely pushing them into envy more than corrective action.

What children hear instead of a motivation speech is the painful message that they’re not enough for you. That you don’t think they’re smart enough or well-behaved or disciplined enough. That you, the one who is supposed to love them unconditionally, prefer another over them.

Your child was uniquely made, and comparing them to others distorts that beautiful truth. Or, as the saying goes, it robs them of their joy and can lead to a lifelong struggle with the insecurity of never being enough.

You’re getting big

What’s wrong with noticing that your child is so much bigger than when they wore that outfit last month? That’s a good thing, right?

Parents may mean, “Look how much you’ve grown,” or “I can’t believe how fast time is going by.” But for children, especially as they become increasingly aware of their bodies, this comment can land differently than intended.

The occasional neutral observation about growth doesn’t cause devastating harm, but repeated evaluation can. Rather than hearing admiration or mere observation, children may hear an evaluation of their size. Even young kids can begin to internalize that having their body monitored, commented on, or judged is normal, and that is not a lesson you want to teach your children.

Western culture is already obsessed with weight and appearance, so comments about a child’s body, no matter how well-intended or casual, can teach them that their value is tied to how they look rather than who they are in Christ.

In addition, when these body comments come from parents, it can normalize them so your child ingests body comments as valid from anyone and everyone, essentially giving an open door for the world to dictate your child’s self-worth based on appearance only.

You ate more than I did

This phrase often slips out without any intention to shame, but as a simple observation or even in jest. But children are keen observers, and comments about how much they eat can quickly turn toxic.

When adults point out portion sizes or compare their own eating habits to a child’s, kids can misinterpret the messaging. While the comment might be thought of as a nonchalant observation to you, it lands as a criticism and comparison to them. This can affect their eating habits and create a toxic relationship with food. Associating food with criticism or shame may contribute to disordered eating patterns.

As their parent, it’s your duty to provide healthy foods and balanced meals. It’s important that you teach your child about good eating habits and to model normal portion sizes. But rather than commenting on how much your child eats, trust that their growing bodies know what they need. And if you have a concern, talk with your child’s pediatrician.

Give them a hug

It can feel pretty awkward for you when your child is in a social situation where a friendly hug might be expected. Meeting distant relatives for the first time, seeing grandparents after a long time apart, or saying goodbye to a friend after a play date may feel like the proper time for an embrace.

If you’re an outgoing, tactile person, you might feel that it’s natural to hug in these social situations. You might even want to encourage your child to be friendly and develop a habit of open affection.

But when you pressure your child to give physical affection that they’re not comfortable with, you aren’t really teaching them how to be openly affectionate. The message that they’re likely receiving is that their personal boundaries are less important than someone else’s feelings or their own social comfort.

Even when the request comes from a safe and familiar adult, like a parent, being told to “just give them a hug” removes a child’s autonomy over their own body. And as they mature, it can make it more difficult for them to recognize when something feels wrong or to speak up when their boundaries are crossed.

As you work on this as a parent, it will be important for you to teach your children how to speak up for themselves in a respectful way when the situation arises. For example, it will be beneficial for you to teach your child to say something like, “I am not ready for a hug right now.” Or, “I can give you a high five.”

Stop crying

For years, society has told children to “stop crying.” On the surface, it’s seen as an attempt to get the child to learn emotional regulation. It’s meant to calm a tense situation. But under those surface-level goals lies a toxic concept.

By telling your children to “stop crying,” you are denying them the right to feel and react authentically. You are dismissing or minimizing their experiences and telling them that their tears need to be stopped so that those around them aren’t uncomfortable.

Healthy emotional regulation is different than silencing emotions. Regulation invites children to acknowledge their feelings and guides them through them. With repeated orders to simply squelch their tears, children will eventually see their emotions as something that must be hidden rather than naturally expressed. And while parents might look at this as emotional regulation, in truth, it’s emotional suppression.

Seeing your child cry is an opportunity to validate feelings, empathize, and teach proper emotional expression. Asking an emotional child questions can teach them to more readily identify why they are emotional in the first place. This will lead to an opportunity for them to actually process a triggering situation and learn from it. Suppressing emotions will eventually lead to negative self-worth.

Godly parenting

The gift of parenthood also comes with responsibility. Many parents like to quote the first part of Ephesians chapter 6, where children are told to obey their parents in the Lord, because it is right. It tells children to “Honor your father and mother”. But the directive doesn’t stop there. The Bible holds both sides responsible for the health of the parent-child relationship.

Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord – Ephesians 6:4, NIV

That verse is key.

Scripture doesn’t give parents unchecked authority as many may think. It places a clear responsibility on them to not provoke and to instruct and discipline with love. Colossians 3:20-21 also tells parents not to embitter their children so they will become discouraged (NIV).

Obedience grows best in a loving and respectful environment, not in the middle of fear and domination. And because of this directive, it’s important to choose your words prayerfully and wisely.

In Matthew 12:36, Jesus says that people will have to give an account for every “idle word” they speak. Idle words aren’t always cruel or even intentional, but they are still damaging. And in parenting, they’re often thoughtless, habitual phrases spoken without a second thought but with great consequence.

Therapy

If you grew up in a household that used these and other toxic phrases, you might use them too. Without forethought or concern for consequences, you just repeat what you’ve been told and what has been modeled for you.

But with maturity and knowledge comes the obligation to do better than you were given. And now you know. You know that these phrases that spill from your mouth out of habit and history are not benign or neutral but are toxic and potentially harmful to your children.

If you need help identifying areas in your own upbringing that are affecting your parenting, please contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or another capable counselor in our online directory.

Together, you and your therapist can rewind your life, identify the areas that left an impression on you, and that are still shaping you as a parent and person.

item.title: Breaking the Cycle: How Family Issues Shape Mental Health Across Generations
item.description:
Family issues have a distinct way of echoing through time. Unresolved conflict, unspoken pain, or unhealthy patterns in one generation likely resurface in the next. The result is the shaping of a generation in how they understand relationships, process emotions, and view themselves. Family dynamics and mental health are connected, as seen in daily interactions. These interactions may be how they respond to stress, or the beliefs they carry about their worth in the future.

Whether it is recognized or not, what gets passed from one generation to the next shows up in real and lasting ways. The weight of those effects can quietly shape how a person sees themselves, how they relate to others, and whether they believe change is even possible. Understanding connection is the first step toward breaking a cycle that no longer serves anyone.

Proverbs instructs people on the importance of showing children good ways of living. “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” (Proverbs 22:6, NIV) Everyone should consider this to help each generation grow up well.

The Weight of What Gets Passed Down

It’s not just recipes or photo albums that families pass down from previous generations. Unaddressed trauma, patterns of communication, and coping mechanisms are also handed down — often without anyone realizing what is happening. A parent who learned to suppress emotions may raise children who do the same, and a grandparent’s anxiety about finances can create a legacy of scarcity.

These patterns become so familiar that they feel like personality traits rather than learned behaviors. What makes this process difficult is that many of the behaviors are never spoken out loud. They are absorbed through observation, quiet signals, and repeated responses that communicate what is acceptable.

Family issues that are handed down can significantly impact mental health. When children grow up in homes with high levels of conflict, emotional neglect, or inconsistent caregiving, they are more likely to experience anxiety, depression, and difficulty forming healthy relationships in adulthood.

This leads to a lens that can shape how individuals interpret the world, depending on their family environment. A lens built by unresolved family issues can distort perceptions of safety, trust, and belonging for years to come. But we have hope in God’s promises: “The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.” (Psalm 34:18, NIV)

When Silence Becomes the Loudest Message

Avoiding difficult conversations is one of the most common family issues that affects mental health throughout generations. Families who develop unspoken rules about discussion tend to push certain topics under the surface. This influences behavior and emotional response in ways that feel confusing to those who are experiencing grief, addiction, mental illness, abuse, or simple disappointments.

When children grow up in environments where emotions are dismissed or minimized, they find it difficult to identify and express their own feelings as adults. This may lead them to experience emotional numbness, difficulty setting boundaries, or have feelings of intense shame when they experience strong emotions. Instead of protecting the family, the silence has created an isolation that leaves each generation to face its own challenges alone rather than together.

Christian counselors work with individuals who are beginning to recognize how family patterns of silence have shaped their mental health. This process encourages the understanding that vulnerability isn’t weakness and that naming pain doesn’t make it worse. Christian counselors emphasize that God’s design for family includes honesty, communication, and mutual support.

The concepts of identifying false beliefs and working with people are biblical. “Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to your neighbor, for we are all members of one body.” (Ephesians 4:25, NIV) This guides us and gives us hope in the process.

The Pressure to Repeat or Reject

Family issues that remain unaddressed will present difficult choices for future generations. These individuals can repeat the patterns they have witnessed or reject them entirely, but each choice will come with challenges. They find themselves repeating the patterns that create the same painful dynamics they have experienced. Rejecting everything about it can cause an individual to overreact and create new problems in their attempt to avoid old ones.

Adults who experience harsh discipline either replicate it with their own children or pivot to the opposite extreme, leaving them unable to set any boundaries. The underlying issue is the need to develop a thoughtful, intentional approach to family relationships based on health rather than rejection. However, neither of these approaches will address that underlying issue, so the healing process can’t begin.

The challenge of choosing to repeat or reject the patterns doesn’t just stop at parenting. Career choices, financial decisions, spiritual practices, and romantic relationships can become battlegrounds in which individuals either reenact or rebel against the family patterns of their past. Those who grew up in a home where faith was a tool of control often walk away from it, and others hold on tightly without ever examining what they actually believe.

Christian counselors help individuals navigate this terrain by exploring a path of healing and transformation, one that honors what was good while releasing what was harmful. This isn’t about assigning blame to the previous generation. It is about developing an honest understanding of where certain patterns came from and making a clear decision about where they will stop.

Creating New Patterns for Future Generations

To break generational cycles of family issues, individuals must be intentional, put in effort, invest time, practice self-awareness, and sometimes seek professional support. The starting point is recognizing that what feels normal isn’t necessarily healthy, and choosing a different path isn’t a betrayal of family.

Through this process, individuals will need to examine beliefs, behaviors, and emotional responses with honesty. They must learn to identify which patterns support well-being and which perpetuate harm.

Seeking professional help when family issues have created lasting impacts on mental health is important in processing pain, developing new skills, and building healthier patterns. This can feel unfamiliar at first, like trying to operate with an entirely different set of tools that includes emotional honesty, appropriate boundaries, and the capacity to give and receive support.

It is important to note that the work put into creating new patterns takes time. Patterns do not shift overnight after years of building. This is simply the nature of meaningful change, not an indication of failure.

The goal is to learn how to address the challenges that every family and generation faces. When family issues come into the light, they are met with appropriate support and discussed with compassion, and they no longer have the strength to dictate the future. Christian counselors work with families to create environments where mental health can flourish, patterns shift, and future generations develop tools for healing the pain that they inherited.

Isaiah reminds us how God does new things, even when we don’t expect it:

See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it? I am making a way in the wilderness and streams in the wasteland. – Isaiah 43:19, NIV

Learn to Break the Cycle of Family Issues

Family issues and mental health across generations have a connection that is both heavy and full of promise. It is sobering because it reveals how deeply past pain can reach into the present. It is hopeful because it shows that change is possible. With awareness, support, and intentional effort, families can create a new dynamic that promotes mental health rather than undermines it.

The cycle can be broken, and inheritance can change. Future generations do not have to receive a legacy of pain when they are given the tools to obtain the legacy of healing, resilience, and hope in Christ, transforming love. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” (2 Corinthians 5:17, NIV)

If family issues have shaped your mental health from past generations, you do not have to navigate the situation alone. Christian counselors are trained to help individuals understand the complex ways that family issues shape mental health and well-being.
